---
title: "Preface"
---

Music theory for people who already write code.

This book assumes you are at ease with arrays, functions, maps, and threads, and
that you cannot read a note. Those two facts together are unusual enough that
most music teaching serves you badly. Beginner material spends chapters on
things you grasped in a paragraph. Reference material assumes a decade of
notation you never acquired.

Sonic Pi closes the gap. It is a live coding environment where music is written
as Ruby, which means every musical idea in this book can be handed to you as
something you run, hear, and then take apart.

## How the course works

Each lesson takes one musical idea, encodes it as data, plays it, and asks you
to change something and listen to what happened. The programming stays
deliberately ahead of the theory so your existing skills carry the load.

- **Sound first, name second.** You hear an interval, a cadence, a mode before
  anyone tells you what it is called.
- **Music is data.** A note event carries pitch, onset, duration, amplitude, and
  articulation. Everything else is a function over those.
- **Score and renderer stay separate.** The composition is content. The playback
  function is interpretation. Changing one should not touch the other.
- **Every lesson ends with something worth hearing.** If the last snippet in a
  lesson is a bare test tone, the lesson is broken.
- **Notation arrives late and on demand.** You learn the staff after you already
  understand pitch and duration as numbers, which makes it a decoding exercise
  rather than a wall.
- **Ear training runs in parallel.** Ten minutes most days, using drills you
  wrote yourself, from Part 2 onwards.

## What this is not

This is not the [Sonic Pi tutorial](https://sonic-pi.net/tutorial.html). That one
teaches programming and uses music as the reward, and it is good at that. Here
the programming is assumed. Ruby idioms get a short note the first time they
appear and no more than that, collected in [Ruby for non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd)
for anyone arriving from another language.

It is also not a substitute for playing an instrument. Nothing here will teach
your hands anything. What it will teach you is what musicians are doing and why,
in a representation you can inspect.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week gets you through the 58 lessons in about fifteen weeks,
with the capstones after that.

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Reread the last four lessons and rebuild one example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play. Use only what you have learned so far and make something you like. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from your own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, add no new theory. Finish a transcription instead. Theory
sticks when you use it under pressure, and the pressure comes from wanting the
thing to sound right.
